title: The light that entered Krishna
hookLine: a light rises from the fallen king and enters Krishna, and Yudhishthira finishes his rite
carry: what the mind dwells on, it reaches

lines: A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.
cards: Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun.
Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him.
It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed.

teach.b: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The Mahabharata shows it and moves on. But Hindus asked the question, and a later scripture, the Bhagavata Purana, has Yudhishthira ask it out loud.

teach.h: NARADA: HE FIXED HIS MIND ON KRISHNA.
teach.b: The sage Narada answers: some came to Krishna through love, some through fear, and Shishupala through hatred, because all of them fixed their minds on him.

He thought about Krishna constantly, and that single-minded attention carried him to Krishna in the end. The Gita puts it as a rule: whatever the mind dwells on at the last, that is where a person goes.

teach.h: THE MIND BECOMES WHAT IT HOLDS.
teach.b: So the teaching is about attention: the mind becomes what it holds. That's why so many Hindus practice remembering God on purpose, a name repeated, a picture kept close, so the mind's resting place is what they love.
Other readers take the light more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. Then the story turns practical.
Yudhishthira has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala and places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi.
The rite is finished, the guests are sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city.
Look back at the week: seva at the Rajasuya, the first honor, gentle speech, held anger, a hundred pardons, the limit, and now the light.

teach.h: WHAT THE MIND DWELLS ON, IT REACHES.
teach.b: Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.

how: In the Bhagavata Purana (Book 7, chapter 1), Narada tells Yudhishthira that Shishupala reached Krishna by fixing his mind on him in enmity, and the Bhagavad Gita (8.6) says a person goes to whatever the mind dwells on at the end. The Mahabharata itself does not explain the light, and readers take it in more than one way.

games.q: you're one of the kings in the hall. Shishupala has fallen, and a light rises from his body. where does it go?
games.why: the poem says the light bowed to Krishna and entered him, and the kings were amazed. it shows this without explaining it.

practice: Think of someone you've had real trouble with, someone who takes up a lot of room in your thoughts. You don't have to change how you feel; just see your attention as a light you've been shining at them.
With each slow breath, gather a little of it back, and set it on something you love. If you pray, rest it on a name of God, said quietly; if not, rest it on someone who makes you glad.

wordCard.voice: Shishupala. Krishna's cousin and fierce opponent, pardoned a hundred times, whose light rose at the end and entered Krishna.

orig.note: Sanskrit tejas: radiance, brilliant energy; a light like this rises from Shishupala and enters Krishna.

carryVoice: Your line: what the mind dwells on, it reaches. Even Shishupala's hatred carried him to Krishna. Tomorrow, a hall that plays tricks. That's the week.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (the radiance rising from Shishupala's body and entering Krishna; funeral rites; Shishupala's son installed; the Rajasuya completed)
Bhagavata Purana, Book 7, chapter 1 (the teaching that fixing the mind on the Lord, even in enmity, leads to him, with Shishupala as an example)
Bhagavad Gita 8.6 (whatever one dwells on at the end, to that one goes)
